claim: Mouse hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells produce multiple pancreatic, gastrointestinal and hypothalamic peptides in addition to exosomes.
source: We report that mouse hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells produce multiple pancreatic, gastrointestinal and hypothalamic peptides in addition to exosomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data showing co-expression of multiple peptides (Figure 1a,b) and exosomal markers (Figure 4a-d), along with ELISA and secretion assays (Figure 2).

claim: A subpopulation of hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells can be generated through cell sorting and selection according to insulin promoter activity.
source: Through cell sorting and selection according to insulin promoter activity, we generated a subpopulation(s) of these cells which formed 3D spherical structure with combined features of hypothalamic neurospheres and pancreatic islets.
evidence: This claim is supported by FACS data (Figure 1e) and microscopy images (Figure 1d) showing successful isolation of insulin promoter-active cells.

claim: Insulin promoter-selected hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells form 3D spherical structures with combined features of hypothalamic neurospheres and pancreatic islets.
source: Through cell sorting and selection according to insulin promoter activity, we generated a subpopulation(s) of these cells which formed 3D spherical structure with combined features of hypothalamic neurospheres and pancreatic islets.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data showing expression of both pancreatic islet markers and neural stem cell markers (Figure 3a-b, Figure 3—figure supplements 1-2).

claim: Peripheral implantation of hypothalamic islet spheres in streptozotocin-induced diabetic mice leads to remarkable improvements in general health and survival.
source: Through testing streptozotocin-induced pancreatic islet disruption and fatal diabetes, we found that peripheral implantation of these spheres in mice led to remarkable improvements in general health and survival in addition to a moderate antidiabetic effect
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data (Figure 6a), body weight measurements (Figure 6b), and behavioral tests (Figure 6g-i).

claim: Peripheral implantation of hypothalamic islet spheres in streptozotocin-induced diabetic mice produces a moderate antidiabetic effect.
source: Through testing streptozotocin-induced pancreatic islet disruption and fatal diabetes, we found that peripheral implantation of these spheres in mice led to remarkable improvements in general health and survival in addition to a moderate antidiabetic effect
evidence: This claim is supported by fasting blood glucose measurements (Figure 5d) and plasma insulin levels (Figure 5e).

claim: The pro-survival and metabolic effects of hypothalamic islet spheres are dissociable to a significant extent.
source: notably these pro-survival versus metabolic effects were dissociable to a significant extent.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analyses (Figure 6c-f) and experiments with insulin-knockdown spheres that retained pro-survival effects despite loss of glucose-lowering effects (Figure 7).

claim: Secretion of exosomes by hypothalamic islet spheres is essential for enhancing survival.
source: Mechanistically, secretion of exosomes by these spheres was essential for enhancing survival while production of insulin was important for the antidiabetic effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments showing that Rab27a knockdown (which inhibits exosome secretion) completely abrogated survival benefits (Figure 7c).

claim: Production of insulin by hypothalamic islet spheres is important for the antidiabetic effect.
source: Mechanistically, secretion of exosomes by these spheres was essential for enhancing survival while production of insulin was important for the antidiabetic effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments showing that insulin knockdown completely abrogated glucose-lowering effects (Figure 7a,b).

claim: Cultured hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells express mRNAs of multiple hypothalamic and gastrointestinal hormones including insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin.
source: Using quantitative PCR, we found that cultured htNSCs expressed mRNAs of multiple hypothalamic and gastrointestinal hormones, evidently including pancreatic hormones such as insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin which led to our research interest of this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative PCR data mentioned in the text.

claim: Some subpopulations of hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells co-express insulin, glucagon and somatostatin.
source: In this background, we did immunostaining revealing that some subpopulations of htNSCs co-expressed insulin, glucagon and somatostatin (Figure 1a,b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining images showing co-localization of these peptides (Figure 1a,b).

claim: Insulin, glucagon, and somatostatin exist in vesicles within the cytoplasm of some hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells.
source: All these peptides were found to exist in the vesicles within the cytoplasm of some htNSCs, according to immunostaining signals in puncta pattern revealed by these peptide antibodies.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining showing puncta pattern (Figure 1a,b).

claim: Insulin-positive vesicles in hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells are often distinct from vesicles positive for glucagon and somatostatin.
source: These peptides could be localized in the same or different vesicles; for instance, insulin-positive vesicles were often distinct from the vesicles positive for glucagon and somatostatin, while the latter two peptides were often co-localized in the same vesicles (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining images showing differential vesicle localization (Figure 1a,b).

claim: Glucagon and somatostatin are often co-localized in the same vesicles in hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells.
source: These peptides could be localized in the same or different vesicles; for instance, insulin-positive vesicles were often distinct from the vesicles positive for glucagon and somatostatin, while the latter two peptides were often co-localized in the same vesicles (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining images showing co-localization (Figure 1a,b).

claim: Insulin is present mostly in large dense-core vesicles (LDCV) in hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells.
source: Using large dense-core vesicles (LDCV) and synaptic-like microvesicles (SLMV) markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), we revealed that insulin was present mostly in the LDCV while glucagon and somatostatin were often co-present predominantly in the SLMV.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization analysis with vesicle markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Glucagon and somatostatin are often co-present predominantly in synaptic-like microvesicles (SLMV) in hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells.
source: Using large dense-core vesicles (LDCV) and synaptic-like microvesicles (SLMV) markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), we revealed that insulin was present mostly in the LDCV while glucagon and somatostatin were often co-present predominantly in the SLMV.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization analysis with vesicle markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Approximately 7% of hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells show insulin promoter activity.
source: The Ins promoter activity was found in ~7% of htNSCs, while the Gcg and Sst promoter activities were found in ~2% and~3% of htNSCs, respectively (Figure 1c)
evidence: This claim is supported by Flp recombinase reporter assay data (Figure 1c).

claim: Approximately 2% of hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells show glucagon promoter activity.
source: The Ins promoter activity was found in ~7% of htNSCs, while the Gcg and Sst promoter activities were found in ~2% and~3% of htNSCs, respectively (Figure 1c)
evidence: This claim is supported by Flp recombinase reporter assay data (Figure 1c).

claim: Approximately 3% of hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells show somatostatin promoter activity.
source: The Ins promoter activity was found in ~7% of htNSCs, while the Gcg and Sst promoter activities were found in ~2% and~3% of htNSCs, respectively (Figure 1c)
evidence: This claim is supported by Flp recombinase reporter assay data (Figure 1c).

claim: Among hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells with insulin promoter activation, approximately 25% show co-activation of somatostatin promoter.
source: We found that among htNSCs which displayed Ins promoter activation,~25% of them showed co-activation of Sst promoter, and 20% of them showed co-activation of Gcg promoter.
evidence: This claim is supported by dual Flp/Cre reporter system data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).

claim: Among hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells with insulin promoter activation, approximately 20% show co-activation of glucagon promoter.
source: We found that among htNSCs which displayed Ins promoter activation,~25% of them showed co-activation of Sst promoter, and 20% of them showed co-activation of Gcg promoter.
evidence: This claim is supported by dual Flp/Cre reporter system data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).

claim: Approximately 44% of hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells with glucagon promoter activation show co-activation of somatostatin promoter.
source: We also found that ~44% of htNSCs with Gcg promoter activation showed co-activation of Sst promoter.
evidence: This claim is supported by dual Flp/Cre reporter system data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).

claim: Co-existence of pancreatic hormones in the same cells can be seen in some immature islets of Langerhans.
source: According to the literature (Katsuta et al., 2010; Segerstolpe et al., 2016; Enge et al., 2017; De Krijger et al., 1992; van der Meulen and Huising, 2014; Jeon et al., 2009), co-existence of these pancreatic hormones in same cells could also be seen in some immature islets of Langerhans
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There exists some developmental relationship between hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells and the precursors of pancreatic islets.
source: According to the literature (Katsuta et al., 2010; Segerstolpe et al., 2016; Enge et al., 2017; De Krijger et al., 1992; van der Meulen and Huising, 2014; Jeon et al., 2009), co-existence of these pancreatic hormones in same cells could also be seen in some immature islets of Langerhans, indicating that there exists some developmental relationship between these htNSCs and the precursors of pancreatic islets.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity in co-expression patterns between htNSCs and immature pancreatic islets.

claim: Many hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells express gastrointestinal hormones such as galanin, VIP, CCK and PACAP.
source: In addition to pancreatic peptides, we observed that many of these htNSCs expressed gastrointestinal hormones such as galanin, vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP), cholecystokinin (CCK) and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating peptide (PACAP)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).

claim: Many hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells express hypothalamic peptides such as NPY, AgRP, α-MSH, CRF, GnRH and oxytocin.
source: as well as hypothalamic peptides such as neuropeptide Y (NPY), agouti-related peptide (AgRP), alpha melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH), corticotrophin-releasing factor (CRF), gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) and oxytocin in subcellular vesicles (some examples of these peptide immunostainings are shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).

claim: For any pairs of peptides examined, they were found to co-exist in some hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells.
source: Notably, for any pairs of these peptides, they were always found to co-exist in some of htNSCs, and each of these peptides could be found present in insulin-positive htNSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining observations mentioned in the text.

claim: Each examined peptide can be found present in insulin-positive hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells.
source: Notably, for any pairs of these peptides, they were always found to co-exist in some of htNSCs, and each of these peptides could be found present in insulin-positive htNSCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining observations mentioned in the text.

claim: Insulin secretion substantially increased in insulin promoter-selected hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells compared to pre-selection cells.
source: First, using a luminescent reporter which was known to sensitively report insulin secretion (Burns et al., 2015), we found that insulin secretion substantially increased in these insulin promoter-selected htNSCs compared to insulin secretion from htNSCs of pre-selection (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by luminescent reporter assay data (Figure 2a).

claim: Insulin promoter-selected hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells secrete insulin in a glucose-regulated manner.
source: Using an ELISA which directly measured insulin, we found that these insulin promoter-selected htNSCs secreted insulin in a glucose-regulated manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA measurements showing glucose-dependent insulin secretion (Figure 2b).

claim: High-level glucose (20 mM) leads to approximately 3-fold increase of insulin release from insulin promoter-selected hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells compared to low-level glucose (2 mM).
source: We found that high-level glucose led to ~3 fold increase of insulin release, which dropped to the baseline after glucose returned to the low level.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA measurements (Figure 2b).

claim: Insulin promoter-selected hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells release insulin in response to potassium chloride stimulation.
source: Moreover, we subjected these htNSCs to potassium chloride or arginine, since both are known to stimulate pancreatic insulin secretion; our results confirmed that these htNSCs released insulin in response to either stimulation (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA measurements (Figure 2c).

claim: Insulin promoter-selected hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells release insulin in response to arginine stimulation.
source: Moreover, we subjected these htNSCs to potassium chloride or arginine, since both are known to stimulate pancreatic insulin secretion; our results confirmed that these htNSCs released insulin in response to either stimulation (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA measurements (Figure 2c).

claim: The insulin-secreting activity of insulin promoter-selected hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells is preserved over at least 10 passages of cell culture.
source: The insulin-secreting activity of these htNSCs was preserved over at least 10 passages of cell culture which we monitored.
evidence: This claim is based on monitoring over multiple cell passages.

claim: Insulin secretion increases more than 30 times in spheres compared to monolayer culture of the same number of insulin promoter-selected hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells.
source: Of interest, compared to cells cultured in the monolayer (Figure 2b), insulin secretion increased >30 times by the same number of cells in the spheres (Figure 2d), suggesting that the 3D spheroid structure is important for optimizing insulin production and secretion.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing ELISA measurements between monolayer (Figure 2b) and sphere cultures (Figure 2d).

claim: The 3D spheroid structure is important for optimizing insulin production and secretion in hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells.
source: Of interest, compared to cells cultured in the monolayer (Figure 2b), insulin secretion increased >30 times by the same number of cells in the spheres (Figure 2d), suggesting that the 3D spheroid structure is important for optimizing insulin production and secretion.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the substantial increase in insulin secretion in 3D spheres compared to monolayer culture.

claim: Hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres show a similar pattern of insulin secretion in response to glucose compared to pancreatic islets.
source: Also, compared to pancreatic islets, these htNSCs spheres showed a similar pattern of insulin secretion in response to glucose, although the capacity was much less comparable to that of pancreatic islets if according to the same number of cells (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing insulin secretion patterns between htNSC spheres and pancreatic islets (Figure 2d).

claim: The insulin secretion capacity of hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres is much less than that of pancreatic islets when comparing the same number of cells.
source: Also, compared to pancreatic islets, these htNSCs spheres showed a similar pattern of insulin secretion in response to glucose, although the capacity was much less comparable to that of pancreatic islets if according to the same number of cells (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing insulin secretion levels between htNSC spheres and pancreatic islets (Figure 2d).

claim: Hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres secrete somatostatin.
source: Besides, some htNSCs in these spheres preserved the features of somatostatin and glucagon secretion, whether they responded to glucose or not (Figure 2e,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA measurements (Figure 2e).

claim: Hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres secrete glucagon.
source: Besides, some htNSCs in these spheres preserved the features of somatostatin and glucagon secretion, whether they responded to glucose or not (Figure 2e,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA measurements (Figure 2f).

claim: Hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres secrete VIP in a glucose-stimulated manner.
source: Moreover, as exemplified in Figure 2g–i, these spheres had the capability of secreting other pancreatic/gastrointestinal peptides such as VIP, CCK and PACAP in glucose-stimulated or glucose-inhibited manners.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA measurements (Figure 2g).

claim: Hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres secrete CCK.
source: Moreover, as exemplified in Figure 2g–i, these spheres had the capability of secreting other pancreatic/gastrointestinal peptides such as VIP, CCK and PACAP in glucose-stimulated or glucose-inhibited manners.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA measurements (Figure 2h).

claim: Hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres secrete PACAP.
source: Moreover, as exemplified in Figure 2g–i, these spheres had the capability of secreting other pancreatic/gastrointestinal peptides such as VIP, CCK and PACAP in glucose-stimulated or glucose-inhibited manners.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA measurements (Figure 2i).

claim: Insulin is globally and widely present in hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres, distributed both in the center and periphery.
source: As expected, insulin was globally and widely present in these htNSC spheres, which were distributed both in the center and periphery, slightly differing from pancreatic islets in which insulin-positive cells were more in the center than the periphery.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data (Figure 3a-b).

claim: Hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres contain higher percentages of somatostatin-positive cells compared to pancreatic islets.
source: Also compared to pancreatic islets, these htNSC spheres contained higher percentages of somatostatin-positive cells but similar percentages of glucagon-positive cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing immunostaining quantification between htNSC spheres and pancreatic islets (Figure 3a-b, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres contain similar percentages of glucagon-positive cells compared to pancreatic islets.
source: Also compared to pancreatic islets, these htNSC spheres contained higher percentages of somatostatin-positive cells but similar percentages of glucagon-positive cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparing immunostaining quantification between htNSC spheres and pancreatic islets (Figure 3a-b, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: Somatostatin-positive cells are distributed in the periphery of hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres.
source: Also, while glucagon- and somatostatin-positive cells were distributed typically in the periphery of pancreatic islets (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–b), it was the case for somatostatin but not for glucagon in these htNSC spheres (Figure 3a–b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining showing spatial distribution (Figure 3a-b).

claim: Glucagon-positive cells are not preferentially distributed in the periphery of hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres.
source: Also, while glucagon- and somatostatin-positive cells were distributed typically in the periphery of pancreatic islets (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–b), it was the case for somatostatin but not for glucagon in these htNSC spheres (Figure 3a–b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining showing spatial distribution (Figure 3a-b).

claim: Hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres express pancreatic islet biomarkers including PC1/3, GLUT2, KIR6.2, and NKX2.2.
source: In addition, we examined pancreatic islet biomarkers including proprotein convertase 1 (PC1/3), glucose transporter 2 (GLUT2), ATP-sensitive K+ channel KIR6.2, and NKX2.2. The results showed that all these biomarkers were widely expressed in these htNSC spheres (Figure 3a–b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–b)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data (Figure 3a-b).

claim: Hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres strongly and universally express NSC biomarkers Sox2 and nestin.
source: On the other hand, unlike the pancreatic islets which barely expressed NSC biomarkers Sox2 and nestin, both biomarkers were strongly and universally expressed in these htNSC spheres (Figure 3a–b, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data (Figure 3a-b).

claim: Pancreatic islets barely express NSC biomarkers Sox2 and nestin.
source: On the other hand, unlike the pancreatic islets which barely expressed NSC biomarkers Sox2 and nestin, both biomarkers were strongly and universally expressed in these htNSC spheres (Figure 3a–b, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–2)
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: When insulin-positive cells are depleted, the remaining hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells can still effectively form spheres.
source: Of interest, when insulin-positive cells were mostly missing, the remaining cells still effectively made spheres; in contrast, when either somatostatin- or glucagon-positive cells were mostly missing, despite that a lot of insulin-producing cells were present, these cells failed to form any spheres (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell ablation experiments (Figure 3c).

claim: When somatostatin-positive cells are depleted, the remaining hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells fail to form spheres.
source: Of interest, when insulin-positive cells were mostly missing, the remaining cells still effectively made spheres; in contrast, when either somatostatin- or glucagon-positive cells were mostly missing, despite that a lot of insulin-producing cells were present, these cells failed to form any spheres (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell ablation experiments (Figure 3c).

claim: When glucagon-positive cells are depleted, the remaining hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells fail to form spheres.
source: Of interest, when insulin-positive cells were mostly missing, the remaining cells still effectively made spheres; in contrast, when either somatostatin- or glucagon-positive cells were mostly missing, despite that a lot of insulin-producing cells were present, these cells failed to form any spheres (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell ablation experiments (Figure 3c).

claim: The co-presence of somatostatin- and glucagon-positive cells is crucial for forming spheres and maintaining insulin-positive cells.
source: Thus, the co-presence of somatostatin- and glucagon-positive cells is crucial for making spheres and keeping insulin-positive cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cell ablation experiments showing sphere formation failure when these cell types are depleted (Figure 3c).

claim: Exosomal biomarkers CD81 and TSG101 are strongly expressed in more than 90% of cells in hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres.
source: As shown in Figure 4a–b, we confirmed that both CD81 and TSG101 were strongly expressed in >90% of cells in these htNSC spheres, but these biomarkers were barely detected in pancreatic islets.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining quantification (Figure 4a-b).

claim: Exosomal biomarkers CD81 and TSG101 are barely detected in pancreatic islets.
source: As shown in Figure 4a–b, we confirmed that both CD81 and TSG101 were strongly expressed in >90% of cells in these htNSC spheres, but these biomarkers were barely detected in pancreatic islets.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining quantification (Figure 4a-b).

claim: Hypothalamic stem/progenitor cell spheres secrete a considerably high amount of exosomal miRNAs.
source: As shown in Figure 4c–d, these htNSC spheres secreted a considerably high amount of exosomal miRNAs while pancreatic islet cells barely did so.
evidence: This claim is supported by small RNA bio-analyzer assay (Figure 4c-d).

claim: Pancreatic islet cells barely secrete exosomal miRNAs.
source: As shown in Figure 4c–d, these htNSC spheres secreted a considerably high amount of exosomal miRNAs while pancreatic islet cells barely did so.
evidence: This claim is supported by small RNA bio-analyzer assay (Figure 4c-d).

claim: The great omentum is a suitable location for peripheral implantation of hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells with more than 50% cell survival over a month.
source: As we continued to try other peripheral locations, we found that the great omentum was a suitable choice of implantation, with >50% implanted cell survival over a month.
evidence: This claim is supported by cell survival analysis of implants (Figure 5b).

claim: Approximately 50% of implanted hypothalamic stem/progenitor cells survive over 1 month in the great omentum.
source: As shown, about 50% of implanted cells survived over 1 month (Figure 5b), and these surviving cells were also positive for insulin promoter-driven mCherry (Figure 5c).
evidence: This claim is supported by sectional analysis of implants (Figure 5b).

claim: Surviving implanted cells in the great omentum are positive for insulin promoter-driven mCherry.
source: As shown, about 50% of implanted cells survived over 1 month (Figure 5b), and these surviving cells were also positive for insulin promoter-driven mCherry (Figure 5c).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging (Figure 5c).

claim: Fasting blood glucose dropped below 300 mg/dL in a majority of STZ mice with hypothalamic islet implantation shortly after implantation.
source: As shown in Figure 5d, while overnight fasting blood glucose remained 350–500 mg/dL in majority of sham-operated STZ mice, blood glucose dropped below 300 mg/dL in a majority of mice with htNSCPGHM implantation shortly after implantation, and many of them were lower than 250 mg/dL.
evidence: This claim is supported by blood glucose measurements (Figure 5d).

claim: The hypoglycemic effects of hypothalamic islet implantation remain for weeks or throughout the follow-up in STZ mice.
source: These therapeutic effects remained for weeks or throughout the follow-up.
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal blood glucose measurements (Figure 5d).

claim: Approximately 25% of experimental mice did not show an appreciable hypoglycemic effect from hypothalamic islet implantation.
source: Although a portion of animals (~25% of experimental mice) did not show an appreciable hypoglycemic effect, it was revealed at the end of the experiment that cells in the implants survived poorly in these mice.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of treatment response variability.

claim: Poor cell survival in implants correlates with lack of hypoglycemic effect in STZ mice.
source: Although a portion of animals (~25% of experimental mice) did not show an appreciable hypoglycemic effect, it was revealed at the end of the experiment that cells in the implants survived poorly in these mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that non-responders had poor cell survival.

claim: Average plasma insulin levels in cell-implanted STZ mice are higher than levels in sham controls.
source: As shown in Figure 5e, average plasma insulin levels in cell-implanted STZ mice were in general higher than the levels in sham controls, although they were still much below the reference of normal mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by plasma insulin measurements (Figure 5e).

claim: Plasma insulin levels in cell-implanted STZ mice are still much below the levels of normal mice.
source: As shown in Figure 5e, average plasma insulin levels in cell-implanted STZ mice were in general higher than the levels in sham controls, although they were still much below the reference of normal mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by plasma insulin measurements (Figure 5e).

claim: Hypothalamic islet implantation does not induce regeneration of pancreatic islets in STZ mice.
source: Through rigorous examination, we confirmed that pancreatic islets were similarly damaged between cell implantation and sham controls (Figure 5f,g), indicating that the effect of this treatment was not due to pancreatic islet protection in this STZ model.
evidence: This claim is supported by pancreatic histology analysis (Figure 5f,g).

claim: Mouse survival rate remarkably increased by hypothalamic islet implantation in STZ diabetes model.
source: Our results showed that mouse survival rate remarkably increased by this treatment (Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve analysis (Figure 6a).

claim: The majority of death in sham-operated STZ mice occurred within 40 days after STZ injection.
source: While the majority of death occurred within 40 days after STZ injection in the sham group, death was greatly avoided when htNSCPGHM islets were implanted.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data (Figure 6a).

claim: Death was greatly avoided when hypothalamic islets were implanted in STZ mice.
source: While the majority of death occurred within 40 days after STZ injection in the sham group, death was greatly avoided when htNSCPGHM islets were implanted.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data (Figure 6a).

claim: Hypothalamic islet implantation improved body weight in STZ mice.
source: Improvement of general health by this treatment was also reflected by improved body weight (Figure 6b).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements (Figure 6b).

claim: There is a lack of correlation between hyperglycemia and survival in sham STZ mice.
source: As shown in Figure 6c, there was a lack of correlation between hyperglycemia and survival in sham STZ model, suggesting that death of STZ mice was not simply a result of hyperglycemia when blood glucose levels were very high.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis (Figure 6c).

claim: Death of STZ mice is not simply a result of hyperglycemia when blood glucose levels are very high.
source: As shown in Figure 6c, there was a lack of correlation between hyperglycemia and survival in sham STZ model, suggesting that death of STZ mice was not simply a result of hyperglycemia when blood glucose levels were very high.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of correlation between blood glucose and survival.

claim: There is only a tendency of relationship between blood glucose and survival in sphere-treated STZ mice.
source: While the sphere-treated STZ mice had a moderate reduction in hyperglycemia (they were still diabetic) and a much greater improvement of survival, the correlation analysis revealed only a tendency of relationship between blood glucose and survival (Figure 6d)
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis (Figure 6d).

claim: The limited benefit of blood glucose drop might not be most important for the improved survival of sphere-treated STZ mice.
source: While the sphere-treated STZ mice had a moderate reduction in hyperglycemia (they were still diabetic) and a much greater improvement of survival, the correlation analysis revealed only a tendency of relationship between blood glucose and survival (Figure 6d), indicating that the limited benefit of blood glucose drop might not be most important for the improved survival of these mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the weak correlation between blood glucose reduction and survival improvement.

claim: There is a lack of clear correlation between blood insulin level and survival in sham STZ mice.
source: In terms of blood inulin, there was also a lack of clear correlation between its level and the survival in sham STZ mice (Figure 6e).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis (Figure 6e).

claim: The correlation between insulin and survival is marginally significant in sphere-treated STZ mice.
source: However, in sphere-treated STZ mice, the correlation between insulin and survival was marginally significant (Figure 6f), suggesting that elevation in blood insulin could have a partial contribution to the improved survival of these mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis (Figure 6f).

claim: Elevation in blood insulin could have a partial contribution to the improved survival of sphere-treated STZ mice.
source: However, in sphere-treated STZ mice, the correlation between insulin and survival was marginally significant (Figure 6f), suggesting that elevation in blood insulin could have a partial contribution to the improved survival of these mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the marginally significant correlation between insulin and survival.

claim: Sphere-implanted STZ mice showed much less declines in muscle strength compared to STZ sham mice.
source: We also subjected a group of implanted mice to a battery of behavioral tests, and as shown in Figure 6g–i, spheres-implanted STZ mice showed much less declines in muscle strength, treadmill running capability and voluntary locomotion, compared to STZ sham mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by grip strength test data (Figure 6g).

claim: Sphere-implanted STZ mice showed much less declines in treadmill running capability compared to STZ sham mice.
source: We also subjected a group of implanted mice to a battery of behavioral tests, and as shown in Figure 6g–i, spheres-implanted STZ mice showed much less declines in muscle strength, treadmill running capability and voluntary locomotion, compared to STZ sham mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by treadmill test data (Figure 6h).

claim: Sphere-implanted STZ mice showed much less declines in voluntary locomotion compared to STZ sham mice.
source: We also subjected a group of implanted mice to a battery of behavioral tests, and as shown in Figure 6g–i, spheres-implanted STZ mice showed much less declines in muscle strength, treadmill running capability and voluntary locomotion, compared to STZ sham mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by open field locomotion test data (Figure 6i).

claim: Insulin knockdown in hypothalamic islet spheres completely abrogates the glucose-lowering effect of the therapy in STZ mice.
source: In contrast, due to inhibition of insulin in these spheres, the glucose-lowering effect of this therapy was completely abrogated as observed in both htNSCPGHM-shIns and htNSCPGHM-shIPC groups (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by blood glucose measurements in insulin-knockdown groups (Figure 7a,b).

claim: An elevation of plasma insulin due to implanted hypothalamic islets accounts for the moderate hypoglycemic effect of the treatment.
source: These results suggest that an elevation of plasma insulin due to implanted htNSCPGHM islets accounted for the moderate hypoglycemic effect of the treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the loss of hypoglycemic effect when insulin is knocked down.

claim: Insulin-knockdown hypothalamic islet spheres still provide a dramatic although partially reduced effect in improving survival and general health of STZ mice.
source: To our surprise, these spheres still provided a dramatic although partially reduced effect in improving survival and general health of these STZ mice (Figure 7c) despite that diabetes in these mice was same severe as was STZ control (Figure 7a).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data (Figure 7c) showing maintained survival benefit despite loss of glucose control.

claim: Exosomal inhibition in hypothalamic islet spheres does not significantly affect the glucose-lowering benefit of the therapy.
source: On the other hand, exosomal inhibition in these spheres as represented in htNSCPGHM-shRab group did not significantly affect the glucose-lowering or insulin-elevating benefits of the therapy (Figure 7a,b)
evidence: This claim is supported by blood glucose and insulin measurements in the Rab27a-knockdown group (Figure 7a,b).

claim: Exosomal inhibition in hypothalamic islet spheres completely abrogates the survival-improving effect in STZ mice.
source: On the other hand, exosomal inhibition in these spheres as represented in htNSCPGHM-shRab group did not significantly affect the glucose-lowering or insulin-elevating benefits of the therapy (Figure 7a,b), but it completely abrogated htNSCPGHM spheres from improving the survival of STZ mice (Figure 7c).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data showing loss of survival benefit with exosome inhibition (Figure 7c).

claim: Behavioral improvements from hypothalamic islet treatment are only marginally compromised when insulin is inhibited.
source: As shown in Figure 7d–g, while the treatment of control spheres did greatly improve all these behavioral functions compared to sham-operated STZ group, these improvements only marginally compromised when insulin in these spheres was inhibited but were completely abrogated when exosomes in these spheres were inhibited.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data (Figure 7d-g).

claim: Behavioral improvements from hypothalamic islet treatment are completely abrogated when exosomes are inhibited.
source: As shown in Figure 7d–g, while the treatment of control spheres did greatly improve all these behavioral functions compared to sham-operated STZ group, these improvements only marginally compromised when insulin in these spheres was inhibited but were completely abrogated when exosomes in these spheres were inhibited.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data (Figure 7d-g).

claim: Hypothalamic islet spheres have differential roles in improving metabolic physiology versus general health.
source: Therefore, htNSCPGHM spheres have differential roles in improving metabolic physiology versus general health, and multifaceted secretion of these spheres are mechanistically important for the different aspects of these therapeutic benefits.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of insulin vs. exosome knockdown on metabolic and survival outcomes.

claim: Multifaceted secretion of hypothalamic islet spheres is mechanistically important for different aspects of therapeutic benefits.
source: Therefore, htNSCPGHM spheres have differential roles in improving metabolic physiology versus general health, and multifaceted secretion of these spheres are mechanistically important for the different aspects of these therapeutic benefits.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experiments showing that different secretory products (insulin vs. exosomes) mediate different therapeutic effects.

claim: The hypothalamus is the major site of insulin expression other than islets of Langerhans in the pancreas.
source: Similarities exist between the hypothalamus and pancreatic islets, for instance, the hypothalamus is the major site of insulin expression other than islets of Langerhans in the pancreas, suggesting that these organs have a particular relationship.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about insulin expression sites.

claim: The hypothalamus and pancreatic islets have a particular relationship.
source: Similarities exist between the hypothalamus and pancreatic islets, for instance, the hypothalamus is the major site of insulin expression other than islets of Langerhans in the pancreas, suggesting that these organs have a particular relationship.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity in insulin expression between these organs.

claim: The hypothalamus of adult rodents was recently found to have certain although limited neurogenic activity.
source: The hypothalamus of animals such as rodents was recently found to be another brain region with certain although limited neurogenic activity during the adulthood (Kokoeva et al., 2005; Kokoeva et al., 2007; Pierce and Xu, 2010; Migaud et al., 2010; Pérez-Martín et al., 2010; Li et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2012; McNay et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012; Robins et al., 2013; Sousa-Ferreira et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017; Recabal et al., 2017; Pellegrino et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The hypothalamus of adult mice contains Sox2-positive neural stem cells residing predominantly in the hypothalamic third-ventricle wall and the mediobasal hypothalamus parenchyma.
source: We showed that the hypothalamus of adult mice contained Sox2-positive NSCs (referred to as htNSCs), residing predominantly in the hypothalamic third-ventricle wall and the mediobasal hypothalamus (MBH) parenchyma, which are capable of differentiation into three neural linages (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Hypothalamic neural stem cells are capable of differentiation into three neural lineages.
source: We showed that the hypothalamus of adult mice contained Sox2-positive NSCs (referred to as htNSCs), residing predominantly in the hypothalamic third-ventricle wall and the mediobasal hypothalamus (MBH) parenchyma, which are capable of differentiation into three neural linages (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Hypothalamic neural stem cells can play a role in long-term metabolic control through effects on hypothalamic neural plasticity.
source: These cells can play a role in long-term metabolic control through the effects on hypothalamic neural plasticity, which could be suggested in the context of relevant literature (Pierce and Xu, 2010; Li et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2012; McNay et al., 2012; Scarlett et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Hypothalamic neural stem cells have a key endocrine function through secreting exosomes.
source: Recently, we discovered that htNSCs have a key endocrine function through secreting exosomes and contribute to the hypothalamic control of aging (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Hypothalamic neural stem cells contribute to the hypothalamic control of aging.
source: Recently, we discovered that htNSCs have a key endocrine function through secreting exosomes and contribute to the hypothalamic control of aging (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Diabetic management should require consideration over health-enhancing endocrine factors in addition to blood glucose control.
source: Based on this observation, we suggest that diabetic management should require consideration over health-enhancing endocrine factors in addition to blood glucose control.
evidence: This claim is a suggestion based on the dissociation between survival benefits and glucose control observed in the study.

claim: The antidiabetic effect of hypothalamic islet therapy could be more appreciable for etiological forms of diabetes which are generally much less severe than STZ-induced diabetes.
source: Also, although the antidiabetic effect was relatively moderate in the experimental model of STZ-induced extreme diabetes, it is likely that this therapy could be more appreciable for etiological forms of diabetes which are generally much less severe.
evidence: This claim is speculative, extrapolating from the moderate effect in severe STZ diabetes to potential effects in milder diabetes.

claim: The antidiabetic effect of hypothalamic neural stem cells might provide an explanation for central FGF treatment leading to sustained diabetic remission.
source: We further speculate that the antidiabetic effect of these cells might provide an explanation for the recently-appreciated central FGF treatment in leading to sustained diabetic remission (Scarlett et al., 2016), given that htNSCs contain tanycytes which proliferate in response to FGF stimulation (Robins et al., 2013), and indeed FGF was notably important for maintaining and growing the hypothalamic spheres in our study.
evidence: This claim is speculative, connecting the current findings to prior observations about FGF treatment.

claim: Hypothalamic neural stem cells contain tanycytes which proliferate in response to FGF stimulation.
source: We further speculate that the antidiabetic effect of these cells might provide an explanation for the recently-appreciated central FGF treatment in leading to sustained diabetic remission (Scarlett et al., 2016), given that htNSCs contain tanycytes which proliferate in response to FGF stimulation (Robins et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: FGF is important for maintaining and growing hypothalamic spheres.
source: and indeed FGF was notably important for maintaining and growing the hypothalamic spheres in our study.
evidence: This claim is based on observations during the culture of hypothalamic spheres in the study.
